chapter_en: The Status of the Convert and Its Laws

sections.body_en:
The Sages said (Yevamot 48b): "A convert who has converted is like a newborn child." One of the meanings of this principle is that his sins are forgiven him. As the Sages said, a sage who is appointed to be a rabbi – his rise to greatness atones for his sins. And they learned this from the convert: "Just as the convert – all his sins are forgiven him, so too a sage who has been appointed – all his sins are forgiven him." That is, a person who rises to greatness – the responsibility placed upon him by virtue of his public role makes him a kind of new person, and presumably he is also roused to repent in order to succeed in his new role; therefore his sins are forgiven him. The same applies to one who is appointed Nasi, and likewise to a groom on his wedding day (Yerushalmi Bikkurim 3:3). All the more so are the convert's sins forgiven, for there is no deeper and greater repentance than the choice to join the people of God and to accept the Torah and the mitzvot, in order to bring blessing and redemption to the world. Similarly, the Sages said that after Israel entered into the covenant at Mount Sinai, they were "washed clean of sins" (Shir Ha-shirim Rabba 4:4).

This means that the convert does not need to do specific repentance for transgressions he committed when he was a gentile. Even so, the Sages said that sometimes, as a result of transgressions the convert committed before his conversion, or because he delayed converting, suffering comes upon him. But this is not suffering of punishment but of refinement, for although his sins have been atoned, sometimes an impression of them remains in his soul that hinders him from rising to high levels. Granted, the refinement need not necessarily come through suffering; he can be refined through diligent study of Torah and musar (ethics).1

The sins forgiven to the convert are sins between man and God; but conversion does not cancel obligations the convert owed to other people, whether Jews or non-Jews. All the loans he took – he must repay; and all the damages he caused – he must pay for. And if he was liable to a penalty in a court of his former people, he must pay his penalty. Just as a Jew who was liable to death or lashes is not exempted from this when he repents of his sin (Peninei Halakha, Yamim Nora'im 6:7), so conversion does not exempt the convert from his prior obligations toward his fellows or from penalties imposed upon him in a court of law.2

notes_en.en:
Yevamot 48b: "It was taught: Rabbi Ḥananya son of Rabban Gamliel says: Why are converts in this time oppressed, and sufferings come upon them? Because they did not keep the seven Noahide commandments. Rabbi Yosei says: A convert who has converted is like a newborn child (and therefore he is not punished for what he sinned while still a gentile); rather, why are they oppressed? Because they are not as expert in the fine details of the mitzvot as Israel (and they are punished for what they do not fulfill after the conversion). Abba Ḥanan says in the name of Rabbi Elazar: Because they do not act out of love but out of fear. Others say: Because they delayed entering under the wings of the Divine Presence." As is known, in matters of faith the understanding that "these and these are the words of the living God" is more prominent; therefore, on the one hand, the main view is that of Rabbi Yosei, that a convert who converts is like one born anew, and consequently his sins are forgiven him, as is explained in the Yerushalmi (Bikkurim 3:3). And then, if he suffers, these are sufferings for transgressions he committed after the conversion, somewhat like what the Sages said (Yevamot 47b): "Converts are as hard for Israel as a sappaḥat," because they are not careful in fulfilling the mitzvot; or because he does not fulfill the mitzvot properly out of love of God but out of fear of punishment. Nevertheless, there is truth in the other opinions as well, that sometimes the sufferings come for transgressions he committed while a gentile, as explained above; but these sufferings are sufferings of love, intended to refine the convert from the impression left by transgressions he committed while a gentile, so that he can rise to high levels – similar to what the Sages said, that sometimes the righteous are afflicted with sufferings of love in order to increase their reward (Berakhot 5a, Rashi s.v. "yissurin"; see Peninei Halakha, Yamim Nora'im 6:8).
Responsa Laḥmei Toda 5 (by R. Yisrael Bassan) wrote that just as a minor is not punished by Heaven until the age of twenty (Bavli Shabbat 89b; Yerushalmi Bikkurim 2:1), so a convert who has converted, being like a newborn child, is not punished by Heaven during the first twenty years after his conversion. And so it seems, that the convert's obligation comes gradually, for the study required to internalize the foundations of faith and the mitzvot takes time, and only afterward can he bear full responsibility for fulfilling the mitzvot.

In Sanhedrin 71b the Gemara discusses in which cases the convert is punished for transgressions he committed while a gentile, and its conclusion is that when the punishment remains the same under the laws of Israel, or when under the laws of Israel his punishment is lighter, the convert is judged for a sin he committed while still a gentile; but when the punishment is more severe under the laws of Israel, he is not judged. So wrote the Rambam, Hilkhot Melakhim 10:4. This is difficult, for we learned in Yevamot 48b that the convert is considered as one newly born and his sins are forgiven him. Tosafot (Sanhedrin, ibid., s.v. "ben") explained that through his conversion he is exempted from punishments under the laws of Heaven but remains liable under human law. End quote. The Aḥaronim explained that just as repentance does not exempt a Jew from the punishment imposed upon him by a court – for then it would be an opening for criminals to sin and claim that they had repented – so conversion does not exempt the convert from punishment, even though it is considered for him as repentance that atones for his sins (Ḥavot Ya'ir 79; Yad Shaul YD 241:4; Mishnat Avraham on Sefer Ḥasidim 215). However, even under human law, the courts of Israel judge him only for sins he committed against Israel while he was a gentile, and not for sins he committed against his fellows or against Heaven, as explained in the Gemara in Sanhedrin, ibid., and as the Rambam wrote (Hilkhot Melakhim 10:4): "A Noahide who blasphemed the Name, or worshiped idols, or had relations with his fellow's wife, or killed his fellow, and then converted – is exempt. If he killed a Jew or had relations with the wife of a Jew and then converted – he is liable." One may explain that what he sinned against Heaven, such as through idolatry, is forgiven him through his conversion, but what he sinned in transgressions between man and his fellow is not forgiven (Radbaz, ibid.). However, for transgressions he committed against his gentile fellows, the court of Israel does not judge, because the rules of a gentile court and of a court of Israel are different, and now that he is considered a Jew, a Jewish court is not able to judge him for matters that before the conversion concerned only gentiles. One may add that even if according to the rules of law it would be possible to judge him, a court of Israel does not have the ability to receive witnesses and examine what he did among his former people, and therefore it does not intervene in this. But a debt that he owed – he is obligated to repay, as Sefer Ḥasidim wrote (sec. 691): "Even though they said: 'A convert who has converted is like a newborn child,' nevertheless he pays what he is obligated to pay. And if he killed a person, he needs atonement." Knesset Ha-gedola cited this as halakha (268, Hagahot Ha-Tur 1). And if the court of his former people had already sentenced him to a penalty, according to Rav Algazi in Gufei Halakhot on the Rambam, ibid., it is possible that through his conversion he is like one born anew and is exempt from it; and according to Rav Eliyahu Shama Ha-Levi in Korban Isha, the penalty remains upon him. End quote. And it seems that as long as the court of his former people is known to be fair, its rulings apply to the gentile, for one of the seven Noahide commandments is to establish courts of law, and his conversion does not cancel them.
Responsa Ḥavot Ya'ir 79 wrote that a gentile who found a lost object belonging to a Jew and then converted – since while still a gentile he was not required to return the lost object, after the conversion too he remains exempt from doing so; but if he robbed a Jew and then converted, he must return the stolen object. And according to Rav Meir Arik (cited in Responsa Maharsham 5:81:8), the convert does not need to return the stolen object, because there was 'despair and change of domain' (ye'ush ve-shinui reshut): presumably the Jew despaired of the stolen object, and the conversion is considered a 'change of domain' (and see Yad Eliyahu 40; Beit Yaakov 3. And on the other hand, Birkei Yosef ḤM 34:28, 24; Shevut Ya'akov vol. 1, ḤM 177).

sections.title_en: The Convert Prays in the Wording of Israel
sections.body_en:
Although the convert is not a descendant of the forefathers, in all the prayers and blessings he says, like all of Israel: "Our God and God of our fathers, God of Avraham, God of Yitzḥak and God of Yaakov," and he says concerning the land: "which You gave as an inheritance to our fathers." He likewise says: "who has sanctified us with His commandments and commanded us," and "who has chosen us from all the nations." This is because Avraham our father is the father of Israel and of converts alike (above 1:9). This is what God said to Avraham (Bereishit 17:5): "And your name shall no longer be called Avram, but your name shall be Avraham, for I have made you the father of a multitude of nations." The Sages explained: "In the past you were a father to Aram; now, from here on, you are a father to all the nations" (Yerushalmi Bikkurim 1:4).

The Rambam explained in his responsum to Rabbi Ovadya the convert: "The essence of the matter is that Avraham our father is the one who taught the people, enlightened them and made known to them the true religion and the unity of the Holy One, blessed be He; he spurned idolatry and annulled its worship, and brought many under the wings of the Divine Presence, and taught them and instructed them. And he commanded his children and his household (these are the converts) to keep the way of the Lord, as it is stated (Bereishit 18:19): 'For I have known him, so that he will command his children and his household after him, and they shall keep the way of the Lord, to do righteousness and justice,' etc. Therefore, whoever converts, until the end of all generations, and whoever declares the unity of the name of the Holy One, blessed be He, as it is written in the Torah, is a disciple of Avraham our father, peace be upon him, and they are all members of his household … Thus Avraham our father, peace be upon him, is the father of his worthy offspring who walk in his ways, and the father of his disciples and of every convert who converts." And the land that God gave as an inheritance to Avraham our father, He also gave as an inheritance to all those who convert and walk in his ways.

However, regarding the places in which the miracles done for Israel at the Exodus from Egypt and the like are mentioned, the convert may choose how to say it. If he wishes, he may change the wording and say: "who brought Israel out of Egypt"; and if he wishes, he may say as in the wording of all of Israel: "who brought us out of the land of Egypt," and the like. In practice the custom is always to say as in the wording of all of Israel, since the convert is included in Israel, as it is stated (Yeshayahu 56:3): "Let not the foreigner who has joined himself to the Lord say: The Lord will surely separate me from His people."3

He may also say the blessing "who has not made me a gentile" like all of Israel. Granted, some say that since he was born a gentile he cannot say "who has not made me a gentile," but should rather say "who has made me a convert" (Rema OḤ 46:4). And some say that he should not recite the blessing at all, for the blessing is over one's birth, and not over what the convert did by his choice (Baḥ 7). But in practice, one who wishes to bless like all of Israel, "who has not made me a gentile," may do so; for although he was born a gentile, when he converted it became clear that there was at the root of his soul an Israelite spark by virtue of which he was able to convert, and for this he can give thanks in the wording "who has not made me a gentile" (Nezirut Shimshon). In addition, according to the explanation of the Kabbalists, the blessing is over the Israelite soul that he receives every morning when he awakens from sleep (see Magen Avraham 46:10; Shulḥan Arukh Ha-Rav 4; and others).

notes_en.en:
According to Rabbeinu Tam (Tosafot, Bava Batra 81a, s.v. "le-ma'utei"), a convert cannot lead the zimmun in a way that discharges others of their obligation of Birkat Ha-mazon, because he cannot say "for the desirable, good and spacious land that You favored and gave as an inheritance to our fathers," as cited in the Mishna (Bikkurim 1:4): "These bring [first fruits] but do not recite: the convert brings but does not recite, for he cannot say: 'which the Lord swore to our fathers to give to us.' And if his mother was of Israel, he brings and recites. And when he prays by himself, he says: 'God of the fathers of Israel.' And when he is in the synagogue, he says: 'God of your fathers.' And if his mother was of Israel, he says: 'God of our fathers.'" And Hagahot Maimoniyot (Hilkhot Tefilla 8:20) wrote that according to Rabbeinu Tam the convert also cannot serve as prayer leader (sheliaḥ tzibbur), since his wording is not like the wording of the congregation.
However, already in the Yerushalmi (Bikkurim, ibid.) it is cited that the halakha follows the opinion of Rabbi Yehuda in the baraita, that a convert says "God of our fathers," since Avraham is the father of a multitude of nations; and Rabbi Yehoshua ben Levi said that the halakha follows him, and Rabbi Abahu likewise ruled in practice that a convert should say "God of our fathers." And so the Rambam wrote (Hilkhot Bikkurim 4:3): "The convert brings and recites, for it was said to Avraham: 'I have made you the father of a multitude of nations' – thus he is the father of the whole world, all who enter under the wings of the Divine Presence; and the oath was first made to Avraham that his children would inherit the land." (In Kapot Temarim, Sukka 38a, s.v. "ve-agav," he wrote that the reason for this is that in the future to come the converts will inherit the land.) Most of the Rishonim likewise ruled that the convert prays in the language of Israel: so wrote Rash and Ra'av (in their commentaries on the Mishna, Bikkurim, ibid.), and so wrote Ri in Tosafot, Ramban, Rashba, Rosh and Ritva on Bava Batra 81a, and others. And so the Rambam wrote in his responsum to Rabbi Ovadya the convert (Blau ed. 293). However, regarding the wording about the Exodus from Egypt, he may say "who brought Israel out of Egypt"; but if he wishes, he may say it like all of Israel, for he is included among all of Israel. And so it is ruled in SA OḤ 53:19 that the convert may be a ḥazan using the regular wording, and in 199:4, regarding his saying the regular wording of Birkat Ha-mazon, and consequently he may lead the zimmun. The Aḥaronim agreed. In the Pesaḥ Haggada as well, he says like all of Israel "We were slaves," and the like (Or Ha-ḥayim, Bemidbar 9:14).

sections.body_en:
As a result of the exiles, different customs crystallized in the communities of Israel, relating to halakha and to the wording of the prayers, and it was ruled as halakha that the custom of a place is binding on all its residents. Even one who had been accustomed to Ashkenazi customs, if he moved permanently to a place where they followed Sephardic customs, the customs of the place would apply to him immediately upon his arrival in the new place, whether leniently or stringently (SA YD 214:2; MB 468:14). And such was the law for a convert, who would take upon himself the custom of the place.

In recent generations God has begun to redeem us, and we have gathered from all the exiles to the Land of Israel, and in almost every city and settlement there are immigrants from different exiles; consequently there is no local custom, and the ruling is that each person should continue in the customs of his fathers, both in matters of halakha and in the wording of the prayers.

A convert, who has no ancestral custom, may choose the custom that he prefers, and conduct himself according to it in all matters of prayer and halakha. This position accords with the status of the convert, in whom the aspect of choice stands out more: by his choice he converted, and it is in his hands to decide which custom he wishes to follow.

In choosing a custom, it is advisable for the convert to consult with a rabbi who knows him and his place of residence, so that he can assess in which community he will be able to feel better and advance in Torah and mitzvot. Likewise, it is possible for the convert to choose, as a general rule, to follow one of the customs, but in certain matters to choose to follow the opinion of the majority of poskim or the essential halakha – for example, to choose to follow Ashkenazi customs except for the custom of prohibiting kitniyot (legumes) on Pesaḥ.

If, after the convert has chosen his customs, he wishes to retract and choose a different custom, he may perform 'hatarat nedarim' (annulment of vows) and switch to the custom that seems more suitable to him. However, it is proper that he do this in consultation with his rabbi, for the change may weaken him or members of his family; therefore it is advisable that the 'hatarat nedarim' and the change be done responsibly, out of a comprehensive consideration.

When the convert is a descendant of Jews, it is preferable that he connect to the roots of his Jewish family and follow their custom in all matters, for in this way he continues the heritage of his forefathers and strengthens his connection to the people of Israel. However, he is not obligated to do so, for since he is converting, he is like one born anew, and therefore he may choose the custom he prefers.4

notes_en.en: In Yeḥaveh Da'at 5:33 he wrote: 1) that in the Land of Israel all converts must follow the Shulḥan Arukh, based on the assumption that the custom of the Land of Israel is according to the Shulḥan Arukh, and so members of all communities must conduct themselves; 2) even if the convert's father is from the Ashkenazi communities, since the convert is like a newborn child he has no connection to his father, and he must follow the Shulḥan Arukh. End quote. However, the poskim did not accept his words, and therefore the rabbis of those of Ashkenazi, North African and Yemenite origin continue to follow their customs of many generations. And even among those of Middle Eastern origin, many rabbis did not accept his words. Likewise regarding a convert, he may choose the community he wishes to join (Rav Shlomo Zalman Auerbach in Halikhot Shlomo, Tefilla 5, note 80; Rav Yosef Shalom Elyashiv in Tefilla Ke-hilkhata 4:5; Otzar Piskei Gerim sec. 31, by Rav Peretz). In Halikhot Shlomo, Mo'adim vol. 2, 4:21, and in the notes, he wrote that if a convert took upon himself to join a particular community, he should follow them in all laws and customs. End quote. This advice is good mainly for one who joins a community of members of a single ethnic group, for whom it is good to cleave to all its customs. But one who joins a community that is mixed from members of different groups – sometimes it is better that he choose different customs for different areas; for example, he connects more to the prayer rite of one community, while in halakhic customs he is more comfortable with the customs of another community, whose customs are accepted by most of the people of the place. Likewise, it is possible that he wishes to follow the custom of a particular community but his Jewish wife is from another community; then it is advisable that in matters of kashrut he follow his wife, and if his wife has mitzva-observant parents and siblings, there is room to advise him to follow them in all laws and customs, and thus his children will continue their family heritage. I wrote above that if he is a descendant of Jews it is good that he connect to the roots of his family; and indeed, according to many of the great Aḥaronim, those of the seed of Israel or relatives of Israel have a connection to their forefathers; see Masoret Ha-giyur 5:19-20.

sections.body_en:
It is a mitzva for a Jew who buys eating utensils from a gentile to immerse them in a mikveh. The aim of the mitzva is to elevate the utensil from the level of a utensil intended for ordinary eating, which is accompanied by desire and human weaknesses, to the level of a utensil intended for preparing foods through which Israel can connect to the values of the Torah (Peninei Halakha, Kashrut 31:1). A convert does not need to immerse his utensils, because when he immerses and becomes a Jew, the utensils in his possession are also purified and elevated with him (ibid. 6).5

However, if while still a gentile he used them for forbidden foods, he must kasher them according to the rule: 'As it absorbs, so it expels.' That is, utensils in which he ate cold foods or drinks – he should clean well with water. Utensils in which he cooked or placed hot foods – he should clean and afterward kasher by immersion in boiling water (hag'ala). Utensils in which he baked or roasted foods in the heat of the oven or on the fire – he should kasher by heating to incandescence (libun), in the manner of their use (see in detail Peninei Halakha, Kashrut ch. 33).

Kosher foods that the convert cooked before his conversion are not subject to the prohibition of bishul akum (food cooked by gentiles), for the prohibition of bishul akum is due to the concern that people may come to assimilate among the gentiles (Peninei Halakha, Kashrut 27:6), and there is no concern of assimilation with the one who prepared the dish, since in the meantime he has converted and become a Jew.6

notes_en.en: The Rishonim and Aḥaronim did not write that a convert must immerse his utensils, and the implication is that his utensils do not need immersion but are purified with him. So wrote Shem Mi-Shmuel (Matot 5678) in the name of his father, the Avnei Nezer; Nezer Ha-kodesh YD 17; Responsa Mahari'a Ha-Levi 109; Tzitz Eliezer 8:20; Minḥat Asher 3:66. Granted, in recent generations some were in doubt about this, among them: Darkhei Teshuva 120:4, in the name of Ḥadrei De'a; Maharshag 3:48. And several rabbis of the last generation wrote to immerse them without a blessing. But in practice there is no need to be concerned about this, as emerges from the silence of the Rishonim and Aḥaronim, and so it seems by reasoning.

The convert's utensils require kashering only if he cooked forbidden foods in them; but if he cooked only kosher foods in his utensils, there is no need to kasher them. Granted, the Rishonim disagreed on whether utensils in which a gentile cooked kosher foods become forbidden due to absorption of bishul akum, and the Shulḥan Arukh (YD 113:16) cited the stringent opinion anonymously and the lenient opinion as 'some say.' And the accepted ruling follows the stringent opinion (Peninei Halakha, Kashrut 28:11, note 12). However, when the gentile cooked foods and then converted, there is no concern of assimilation with him, and therefore it is permitted to eat these dishes (Avnei Zikaron 1:88).

sections.body_en:
At the time of conversion the convert becomes obligated in the mitzvot. Therefore, if after the conversion a female convert gave birth to her firstborn son, he is obligated in pidyon ha-ben (redemption of the firstborn), as it is stated (Shemot 13:2): "Sanctify to Me every firstborn, whatever opens the womb among the Children of Israel, of man and of beast; it is Mine," and she indeed gave birth to him when she was "among the Children of Israel." But if she gave birth to him before she immersed for her conversion, even though she had already begun the conversion process, her son is exempt from the redemption of the firstborn. If she gave birth or miscarried while she was a gentile, even though they said, "A convert who has converted is like a newborn child," since her womb has already been opened, the first son she bears after her conversion is not considered 'one who opens the womb,' and he is exempt from redemption (Mishna Bekhorot 46a; SA YD 305:20-21).7

Similarly, if the convert's animal bore a firstborn before he converted, the firstborn has no sanctity, since the mitzva takes effect at the time of birth, and at that time he was not yet obligated in mitzvot. And if it gave birth after he converted, the firstborn is holy (see SA YD 318:5; 321:18).

Similarly, if the convert kneaded his dough before he converted and baked it after his conversion, the dough is exempt from separating ḥalla, since the time of the ḥalla obligation is at the kneading, and at that time he was not yet obligated in mitzvot. And if he kneaded his dough after his conversion, the dough is obligated in ḥalla (Mishna Ḥalla 3:6; SA YD 330:4).

Similarly, if he harvested his field before he converted, even though he had not yet gathered the harvest, he is exempt from leket, shikheḥa and pe'a, since the time of obligation of the gifts takes effect at the harvest, and at that time he was not yet obligated in mitzvot (Mishna Pe'a 4:6; Rambam, Hilkhot Matanot Aniyim 2:9).8

The prohibition of lending at interest applies among Israel, but in loans between Jews and gentiles there is no prohibition of interest. If a gentile lent money to a Jew, and before he converted they calculated how much the Jew must pay for the principal and the interest, and recorded it as a loan, the debt is considered as already collected, and the Jew must return the loan with the interest to the convert. But if they did not calculate it and did not record it as a loan, since he has converted it is forbidden for the convert to collect the interest from the Jew. And if, conversely, a Jew lent money at interest to a gentile, in any case the convert must pay the amount of the loan with the interest, so that people should not cast aspersions on his conversion and claim that he converted in order to be exempt from the interest (Bava Metzia 72a; SA YD 171:1).

notes_en.en: In Peninei Halakha, Likkutim, Mishpaḥa 9:10, it is cited that the poskim disagreed about how to proceed with a firstborn who has no father. Some say that the son should redeem himself after he reaches the age of mitzvot (Rema 305:10; Taz 11; Har Tzvi YD 242). And some say that the court, the rabbi or the grandfather of the firstborn may serve as agents of the firstborn infant and redeem him on the day set by the Torah, which is the thirty-first day, and even recite the blessing over his redemption. And it is preferable to do so, both in order to fulfill the mitzva in its time, and out of concern that the firstborn will forget to redeem himself after he grows up (Shakh 305:11; 20; Arukh Ha-shulḥan 305:13-14). According to this opinion his mother may also redeem him (Meshiv Davar 2:87). And some take both views into account, and redeem him on the thirty-first day without a blessing, and after he grows up he redeems himself again without a blessing (Ḥatam Sofer YD 295). Similarly regarding a firstborn born to a woman who converted while pregnant: even if his father is Jewish, since the son is not attributed to him, according to Beit Yitzḥak EH 1:29:5 the son should redeem himself when he grows up. And so wrote Tzitz Eliezer vol. 9, 28:7. On the other hand, Rav Felder in She'ilat Yeshurun YD 28, regarding a case in which the mother is Jewish and the father a gentile, wrote that the court should redeem him. Similarly, Igrot Moshe YD 1:195 wrote that the mother's father should redeem him. In practice, it is good to take both views into account.

In a case where a doubt arose whether the moment of obligation was before the conversion or after it: when the doubt concerns ritual prohibitions, such as the obligation of the offering of a woman after childbirth, ḥalla, the firstborn of a kosher animal, and the firstborn of a donkey – one must be stringent. And in a doubt concerning money, such as the first of the fleece, the foreleg, cheeks and maw, the money for pidyon ha-ben, and the redemption of the firstborn of a donkey – one may be lenient, for 'the burden of proof is on the one who seeks to extract from his fellow' (Ḥullin 134a-b; SA YD 318:5; 321:18; 330:4). And the Shakh (330:8) wrote that when the obligation is rabbinic, even in matters of prohibition there is doubt whether one must be stringent; therefore, at a time when the mitzva of ḥalla is rabbinic, he should separate ḥalla without a blessing. And according to the Taz (330:3), when the mitzva of ḥalla is rabbinic, in a situation of doubt there is no need to separate it.

sections.title_en: A Convert in His First Days
sections.body_en:
Several poskim wrote that if the convert converted before the end of four hours [of the day], he should say Birkhot Ha-shaḥar and Birkhot Ha-Torah and pray. And if after four hours, he should not pray, but should say only Birkhot Ha-Torah; and if he wishes, he may also say Birkhot Ha-shaḥar, whose time, according to many, is all day. They likewise discussed additional halakhot relating to the day of conversion.

However, in general these detailed halakhot are not practical and are intended mainly for study and for clarifying the parameters of the halakhot, for all matters of obligation here apply only to a convert who is very learned and well versed in the laws of prayer and blessings. But in general the convert does not know the details of the laws of prayer and blessings at the time of conversion, and consequently he is not required to be meticulous in their fulfillment. For the Sages said (Yevamot 47a-b) that before the conversion "we inform him of some of the lighter mitzvot and some of the more stringent mitzvot … and we do not overburden him, and we are not exacting with him." That is, the convert must gradually become accustomed to fulfilling the mitzvot, and if before the conversion he did not become accustomed to fulfilling the laws of prayer and blessings in all their details, he need not pressure himself to fulfill them immediately; rather, he should become accustomed to them according to his ability.9

If there was a mezuza affixed to the doorway of his house at the time he converted: if the convert affixed it while still a gentile, he should remove it and affix it again with a blessing. And if it was affixed by a Jew who lived there before, and remained after he left, there is no need to remove the mezuza, since it was affixed by a resident who was obligated in it.

notes_en.en:
Discussions of the details of halakhic obligations on the day of conversion are cited in contemporary books on conversion. On the time for Shaḥarit prayer see Peninei Halakha, Tefilla 11:4, and on the time for Birkhot Ha-shaḥar, ibid. 9:4. Regarding Purim, in the Yerushalmi Megilla (2:3), in the course of the discussion about a resident of an unwalled town who visited a walled city and vice versa, the words of Rav Naḥman bar Yaakov are cited: "Accordingly, a convert who was circumcised after the east became light – is already exempt." On this basis Rishonim and Aḥaronim discussed whether one who converted between dawn and sunrise is obligated in the night reading of the Megilla (see Or Zarua 2:369, and Magen Avraham 687:1). But the Aḥaronim wrote (Maḥaneh Ḥayim vol. 3, EH 66; Mikra'ei Kodesh (Frank), Purim 16; and others) that the entire discussion concerns the night, but it is agreed that the obligation of the daytime Megilla reading applies to him, even if he converted in the middle of the day. The reason is that the obligation of time-bound mitzvot does not depend on the person having been obligated at the beginning of the mitzva's time; rather, it suffices that he became obligated during the time of its fulfillment. The same applies to a convert who converted during the days of Sukkot, who is obligated in sukka, and the like.
One who converts during the days of Sefirat Ha-omer should count without a blessing (Pri Ha-aretz 3, OḤ 1; Birkei Yosef OḤ 489:20; Kaf Ha-ḥayim, ibid., 94). Granted, regarding a child who becomes bar mitzva, I wrote (Peninei Halakha, Zemanim 2:7) that if before he became an adult he did not miss any day, he continues to count with a blessing; but that is because he had an obligation to count by virtue of ḥinukh (education in mitzvot). Here, however, where he had no obligation, even if he counted with a blessing before the conversion, he is considered as one who did not count. And if he converts on the first day of the Omer, he should count during the day without a blessing, and on the remaining days with a blessing (Birkei Yosef, ibid.; Kaf Ha-ḥayim, ibid., 95).

sections.body_en:
The Torah commanded that when Israel wish to appoint a king, they should appoint a person born of Israel and not a convert, as it is stated (Devarim 17:15): "You shall surely set over yourself a king whom the Lord your God shall choose; from among your brothers you shall set a king over yourself; you may not put over yourself a foreigner who is not your brother." The Sages expounded: "from among your brothers" – to exclude the convert (Yevamot 102a).

Although this mitzva is from the Written Torah, and therefore we are unable to understand its full meaning, several reasons can be given for it: 1) The king must rouse the people to observe Torah and mitzvot, and if he is from a foreign background, there is concern that he will turn the hearts of Israel to the ways of the gentiles (Rashbam, Bekhor Shor, Ralbag and Ḥizkuni). It seems one may explain that since the king is burdened and occupied with the affairs of the kingdom, he has no leisure to weigh every action and response properly; therefore there is concern that he will react and command according to his original habits and not as is fitting in Israel. 2) The king must understand the people, especially when he must cope with grave crises, and for this he needs to have grown up from within the people. Therefore the Sages said that the king must also be a native of the land, as it is stated: "from among your brothers" – "and not from outside the Land" (Sifrei, ibid.). 3) The king must be respected and accepted in Israel, so that his words will be heeded. Especially in difficult times of dispute or war, identification with the king and his leadership preserves the unity of the people and strengthens it in the face of its enemies.

The Sages said that not only the king must be from among Israel, but all positions of authority must be held by Israelites, as it is stated: "'You shall surely set (som tasim)' – all appointments that you make shall be only 'from among your brothers.'" And this refers not only to an important position of authority such as head of a city, but to any role that involves coercion and the power to punish, such as responsibility for supervising the weights in the market, including the authority to punish cheaters at his discretion; and likewise responsibility for distributing water for drinking and for agriculture, where the one in charge has the authority to reduce the water allocation of someone who took more than his share (Kiddushin 76b). For all other honored positions that do not involve authority including the power of coercion and punishment, there is no restriction on appointing converts.

Although all positions of authority are learned from the law of the king, there is a difference between them: in appointing a king one must be careful that both his father and his mother be of Israel (Tosafot, Rashba), for the Sages expounded that the king must be from the choicest of his brothers (Bava Kamma 88a). But for other positions of authority it suffices that his father or his mother be of Israel, as it is stated: "from among your brothers" – and even if only one of his parents is of Israel, he is considered "from among your brothers" (Yevamot 45b; Kiddushin 76b).10

When it is the public who wishes to appoint the convert to the position of authority, he may be appointed. This was the law even at the time when appointments to positions of authority were made by representatives of the kingdom and the heads of families: when they knew that the public wanted the convert, they could appoint him. All the more so when the convert himself is elected in democratic elections by the majority of the public to the position of mayor and the like.

In addition, there is room to say that when society is conducted according to the principles of the democratic conception, according to which authority is limited – all office holders are subject to the law and to procedures, they are nothing but agents of the public, and all appointments are temporary – there is no restriction on appointing converts to positions of authority, since the public has consented to this with a general, principled consent. Rav Yisraeli wrote something similar even regarding the appointment of gentiles (Amud Ha-yemini 12, ch. 5, 8).

notes_en.en:
The distinction between a king and other positions of authority is cited in Tosafot Sota 41b, s.v. "oto"; Rashba, Yevamot 102a; Rabbeinu Baḥya, Devarim 17:15; Sefer Ḥaredim (negative commandments 4, 60). The Ramban (Yevamot 45b) likewise raised this as a second possibility, and so it is implied by the Semag, negative commandments 221. There is a difficulty with their view: how was Reḥavam son of Shlomo fit to be king, when his mother was Na'ama the Ammonite, who was a convert? And how did those who rebelled against David wish to make Avshalom king, the son of Ma'akha, who converted? The Noda Bi-Yehuda (Kamma, ḤM 1) explained that indeed, in appointing a new king both his parents must be of Israel, but one who inherits the kingship from his father does not require that his mother also be of Israel. So wrote the Ḥatam Sofer, OḤ 12 (and in Torat Moshe, Devarim 17:15). And Ḥemdat Yisrael (vol. 1, Mafteḥot Ve-hosafot 93) added that since Reḥavam inherited the kingship only by virtue of his father, when he presumed to reign with greater force than his father, they rebelled against him, and the kingdom was divided. In Mishpetei Uziel (2:42) he explained that the law of the kings of the House of David is special: since the kingship was given to them, even when their mother is not of Israel, they inherit the kingship. And Rabbi Moshe Zakut (in his commentary on the Zohar, Parashat Balak, p. 238) explained that Na'ama herself was not a convert; rather, "her mother, or even her mother's mother, was the one who converted, and Na'ama was conceived and born in holiness, and her offspring are permitted to reign."
Additional opinions: According to the Rambam (Hilkhot Melakhim 1:4), even for a king it suffices that his mother be of Israel, and the Kesef Mishneh explained that the same law applies if only his father is of Israel. And several more Rishonim stated without qualification that if his mother is of Israel he is fit for kingship (Bekhor Shor and R. Ḥayim Paltiel on Devarim 17:15; Tosafot Sota, ibid., in explaining Rashi's view). According to the Ritva (Kiddushin 14a), wherever it was said that his father and mother must be of Israel, 'his father' is precise and 'his mother' is not precise; therefore if his father is of Israel he is fit for kingship. In Ḥiddushei Ha-Ran on Sanhedrin 36a it is explained that if the father is a gentile or both parents are converts, the son is not fit for kingship, but if one parent is of Israel and one parent is a convert, he is fit for kingship. And the Ramban (Yevamot 45b) likewise raised this as the first possibility.
In Kiddushin 76b: "We learned: 'You shall surely set over yourself a king … from among your brothers' – all appointments that you make shall be only 'from among your brothers.' Rav Adda bar Ahava said to him: Even if his mother is of Israel? He said to him: If his mother is of Israel – we read concerning him 'from among your brothers.'" Thus for other 'appointments' (positions of authority) it is agreed that he may be appointed even if only his mother is of Israel. And it is implied that all the more so if only his father is of Israel he is fit, as emerges from the Kesef Mishneh on Rambam, Hilkhot Melakhim 1:4. The law that other positions of authority must be held by an Israelite is also from the Torah, since its source is in the verse; and so wrote the Sefer Ha-ḥinukh 498.

sections.title_en: Appointing a Convert as a Judge
sections.body_en:
One of the positions of authority concerning which the Torah commanded "from among your brothers" is the role of judge, and there are three levels in this. To be one of the twenty-three judges in capital cases, the judge must be of Israelite lineage on both his father's and his mother's side (Sanhedrin 36b; Tosafot s.v. "ḥada"). Likewise in the case of ḥalitza, even though it is not as severe as capital cases, they learned from the verse that it requires that "his name shall be called in Israel," and for this the three judges of ḥalitza must be of Israelite lineage on their father's and mother's side, as it is stated (Devarim 25:8-10): "And the elders of his city shall call him and speak to him … and his name shall be called in Israel: the house of him whose shoe was removed" (Yevamot 102a; SA YD 269:11; EH 169:2).

For monetary cases, which are judged before three judges, since it is a lesser form of authority, it suffices that the judge's father or mother be of Israel, and thereby he is already considered "from among your brothers" and may judge Israelites in monetary cases.

One whose two parents are converts cannot serve as a judge to judge Israelites, but he can serve as a judge to judge converts (Yevamot 102a). He can likewise serve as a judge in proceedings on accepting a convert into Israel.11

And if the public wishes, it may agree to accept upon itself a judge whose two parents are converts or who is himself a convert. And so we find that Shemaya and Avtalyon were the heads of the Sanhedrin even though they were sons of converts, because Israel accepted them upon themselves.12

notes_en.en:
Granted, according to Rashi (Yevamot 102a, s.v. "ger"), a convert may judge his fellow convert even in capital cases, and in monetary cases may judge an Israelite as well. But the vast majority of the Rishonim hold as I wrote above, among them: Tosafot Sanhedrin 36b, s.v. "ḥada"; Rif (Sanhedrin 13b in the Rif's pagination); Rosh (Sanhedrin 4:10); and Rambam (Hilkhot Sanhedrin 11:11). So wrote SA YD 269:11; Levush; Ḥesed La-alafim 4; Sma (ḤM 7:1); and others. Not all of them specified that in capital cases the judge must be an Israelite on both sides, but so wrote Nimukei Yosef, Yevamot 102a, s.v. "dan." Regarding a judge for ḥalitza, the opinion of most Rishonim is that both his parents must be of Israel; but Tosafot (Yevamot 102a, s.v. "le-inyan") wrote that it suffices that his father be of Israel.
Included in the principle that a convert may judge his fellow convert is that he may also serve as a judge for conversion. So wrote the Aderet (Ma'aneh Eliyahu 88); Rav Felder in Naḥalat Tzvi (vol. 1, pp. 226-227); Responsa Beit Mordekhai (ḤM 80, by Rav Mordekhai Fogelman); She'erit Yisrael (YD 22, by Rav Minzberg); Rav Ovadya Yosef (Mishnat Yosef 13:31) [?]; Rav Shlomo Zalman Auerbach, as cited in Dibrot Eliyahu (11:179); and Mar'eh Ha-bazak (9:33). However, some were stringent, because acceptance by Israel is required (Rav Yelov, Shalmei Shmuel 45; and so it is implied by Rav Shlomo Kluger in Tuv Ta'am Va-da'at, YD Mahadura Revi'a'a, 268).

How did they appoint Shemaya and Avtalyon to be Nasi and Av Beit Din of the Sanhedrin? According to the Maharal (Derekh Ha-ḥayim 1:10), Shemaya and Avtalyon themselves were not converts but descendants of converts, and their mother was of Israel. So wrote the Tosafot Yom Tov, ibid., and so wrote the author of the Noda Bi-Yehuda (Doresh Le-Tziyon, end of Derush 3); therefore there was no obstacle at all to appointing them.
And many hold that they were converts. So wrote Knesset Ha-gedola (Hagahot Beit Yosef, ḤM 7:1), and he explained that the public accepted them upon itself, and their acceptance was effective even for capital cases (it seems the meaning is a broad public acceptance, beyond the ordinary acceptance by which the heads of the Sanhedrin were accepted). And so wrote Rav Kalischer in Moznayim La-mishpat (ḤM 7:1), that the public's acceptance was effective even for capital cases; and he explained that presumably the acceptance was by the sages of the study hall in Jerusalem, who agreed to it in the name of all Israel. And so wrote the Tumim (7:1), that it suffices that the sages and the leaders of the public agree that there are none as worthy as they. The Tumim raised a difficulty: public acceptance can be effective only for monetary cases and not for capital cases, and since they sat on the Sanhedrin, it is implied that they also judged capital cases. In his first explanation he wrote that they received the appointment from the Hasmonean kingdom, and just as the kingdom had the authority to execute, so it could also appoint judges to the Sanhedrin even for capital cases. And in his second explanation he wrote that in truth they did not judge capital cases.
And some explained that when the convert is markedly greater than the other rabbis, he may be appointed in the usual manner without special public consent. So wrote Riva in the name of the Semag (Commentary of the Ba'alei Ha-tosafot on the Torah, Parashat Mishpatim, p. 247). And so wrote the Rashbatz (Magen Avot 1:10): "And perhaps since there was none in Israel like him in [knowledge of] the tradition, he was more fitting than all of them. For the Torah disqualified converts only when there are those like them in Israel; but if there are none like them in Israel, they take precedence." So wrote the Ḥida (Birkei Yosef ḤM 7:6); and Ḥemdat Yisrael (vol. 1, Kuntres Ner Mitzva, sec. 89).

sections.title_en: The Roles of Rabbi and Rosh Yeshiva
sections.body_en:
Just as one whose two parents are converts is not appointed to the role of judge, so he is not appointed to the role of a rabbi that involves authority, such as a city rabbi who has powers and the ability to coerce, for example to grant a kashrut certificate or to revoke it. But if the public wishes to choose him, it may. And if he is markedly superior to the other candidates, it is fitting to choose him. And if it is a rabbinic role that involves no authority, but only teaching and guidance, there is no obstacle whatsoever to appointing a convert.

In the role of rosh yeshiva there is sometimes no authority – this is when the yeshiva is a private and not a central institution, and those who wish to come to teach or study in it decide to accept upon themselves the leadership of the rosh yeshiva. But if it is an important yeshiva that serves a large public, the role of rosh yeshiva involves authority, and to the role of rosh yeshiva of such a yeshiva one does not appoint a convert or one whose two parents are converts. But if the public wishes to choose him, it may. And if he is markedly superior to the other candidates, it is fitting to choose him.13

In this law too we encounter the foundation of choice that stands out more in converts; therefore, even for the most talented converts, it is more fitting that they contribute in roles of learning, guidance and creativity, and less in roles that require authority and coercion. And so we find that when Rabban Gamliel was removed from his position as Nasi, they raised the possibility of appointing Rabbi Akiva, who had no equal in greatness in Torah, but they refrained from doing so because he lacked ancestral merit, being the son of converts, and there was concern that Rabban Gamliel's distress would cause him to be punished if he sat on his seat. Therefore they appointed Rabbi Elazar ben Azarya, who was wise and wealthy and also of distinguished lineage – the tenth generation from Ezra the Scribe (Berakhot 27b). "And Rabbi Akiva sat grieving and said: It is not that he is more learned in Torah than I, but that he is the descendant of greater people than I. Fortunate is the person whose ancestors have earned him merit; fortunate is the person who has a peg on which to hang" (Yerushalmi Ta'anit 4:1). But in the end, even though he did not hold a position of authority, Rabbi Akiva was regarded as the greatest of the Tanna'im and the greatest of the Oral Torah, and all the teachings cited in the words of the Sages without the name of their author derive from him. And all the great Torah scholars of the following generation were his distinguished disciples: Rabbi Meir, Rabbi Yehuda, Rabbi Yosei, Rabbi Shimon bar Yoḥai and Rabbi Elazar ben Shamua (Yevamot 62b; Sanhedrin 86a). For Rabbi Akiva's power of innovation surpassed them all, for he would expound upon each and every letter and each and every crown heaps upon heaps of halakhot (Menaḥot 29b), and concerning him they expounded the verse (Yeshayahu 53:12): "Therefore I will give him a portion among the many, and he shall divide the spoil with the mighty" – "This is Rabbi Akiva, who arranged the Midrash of halakhot and aggadot" (Yerushalmi Shekalim 5:1).

notes_en.en:
Some wrote that a convert should not be appointed to the role of local rabbi, rosh yeshiva or mashgiaḥ ruḥani (spiritual supervisor), because these involve authority and coercion (Shraga Ha-me'ir 6:30; Mishneh Halakhot 15:99). According to Igrot Moshe YD 4:26, because of the mitzva of loving the convert one should lean toward leniency; therefore he ruled that a convert may be appointed rosh yeshiva, since it is a role that involves no authority, but is rather like an employer over his workers. So wrote Yabi'a Omer (11, ḤM 2), that it is permitted to appoint a convert as rosh yeshiva, and he added that this involves no authority, but rather his role is to teach Torah to others; and even though he can dismiss students, this is not considered authority, since he does so for the sake of the Torah. And in Igrot Moshe (YD 2:44; 4:26) he wrote that a convert should not be appointed as a kashrut supervisor (mashgiaḥ), because this involves authority to enforce his decisions and to punish refusal. Rav Peretz (Otzar Piskei Gerim sec. 47) permitted it, since he is only the agent of the rabbi. In Tzitz Eliezer 19:48 he held that a convert should not be appointed as gabbai of the synagogue, because this involves authority; but if they chose him, then they have accepted him upon themselves and it is permitted (and he added further reasons). And Rav Fogelman in Beit Mordekhai (ḤM 80) permitted appointing a convert as rabbi of a settlement or community, since the role is essentially not one of authority and coercion, and he brought proofs from several cases in which converts were appointed in Jewish communities.
It seems that in practice, in all matters of the rabbinate and of serving as gabbai there are different aspects: when the essence of the role is to teach and to rule or to organize by consent, one appoints [a convert] even ab initio; and when the essence of the role includes authority and coercion, one does not appoint. But if they wished and agreed, he may be appointed. Likewise, when appointments are made for a fixed term and with limited authority, according to the democratic system, there is room to say that there is no restriction. In any case, there is no obstacle whatsoever to granting converts rabbinic ordination certificates, for today most rabbinic roles, even the most honored, are roles of teaching and organizing by consent, without coercion.
